sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Chronic middle ear infection (otitis media) is one of the most common ear diseases worldwide and is estimated to affect more than 20 million people1. Approximately one quarter of the patients develop cholesteatoma over time – a special form of otitis media characterized by the ingrowth of keratinizing squamous epithelium into the middle ear2–4.

Cholesteatomas often remain undetected for years, and initial symptoms such as tinnitus, purulent otorrhea, or increasing hearing loss usually only appear once the ossicular chain has already been damaged5,6. Patients with cholesteatoma have to be treated with surgery7. Although the standard procedure for mastoidectomy has been shown to be effective, it can be associated with complications such as hearing loss, delayed wound healing, facial nerve paralysis, vertigo, loss of taste, and an increased risk of infection1,8,9. Depending on the clinical situation, mastoidectomy can be performed with or without creation of a radical cavity. sec.title: Ablation of superficial tissue layers on cartilage model using single pulses
sec.p: The histological analyzis supported the OCT measurement data. H&E staining revealed precise ablation of the superficial tissue layer (perichondrium), while the cartilage matrix remained intact throughout (Fig. 2b). Across all tested power settings, the underlying cartilage showed no structural alterations. The outer tissue layers were successfully removed without damaging the cartilage structure beneath.

sec.title: Influence of varying fiber position on the ablation depth
Ablation with overlapping pulses
Laser ablation of human ossicles and cholesteatoma tissue
Discussion
sec.p: In this study, OCT was primarily used to quantify the ablation depth. However, OCT has increasingly been investigated as an imaging modality for middle ear structures. Several studies have shown that OCT can be used to visualize middle ear structures and may help to distinguish cholesteatoma from surrounding tissue48–51. These findings suggest that OCT may not only serve as a quantitative tool but also has potential for intraoperative assessment of middle ear pathology.

In CW mode, heat input accumulates due to continuous energy delivery, whereas in single-pulse mode, the energy is delivered for a short time and the tissue is able to cool down in between pulses. If the pulse duration is within the range of the thermal relaxation time, the effect is limited to the superficial layers53. Studies on gingiva showed significantly broader and deeper thermal influence zones in CW mode, which further supports the use of single-pulse mode for working close to bone24.

sec.title: Conclusion
Preparation and characterization of porcine cartilage models
Human cartilage reference tissue
sec.p: Human tissue samples were taken during clinical operations at the Department of Otolaryngology at the University Medical Center Schleswig–Holstein, Lübeck Campus. The samples were used after approval by the ethics committee (ethics vote: file number 2022–560). We confirm that all methods were performed in accordance with the relevant guidelines and regulations (Declaration of Helsinki). Immediately after collection, the tissue samples were stored in physiological saline solution and processed within two hours for ablation experiments.

sec.title: Ablation experiments
sec.p: Before each ablation was performed, it was necessary to apply a small amount of pig blood to the samples. This also helped to maintain a moist surface and reduce potential drying effects during the measurements. Tissue samples from both porcine cartilage and human tissue were used. The blood was applied using a thin brush, and the surface of the sample was dried with blotting paper before application to ensure the smallest possible and optimal blood layer height25. This enabled reproducible carbonization and simulated realistic surgical scenarios, which in turn allowed the volume removal and ablation depth to be measured. An image was then captured using a camera attachment (EOS 550D, Canon, Japan) on a microscope (Stemi SV8, Zeiss, Germany). The sample was then positioned on an adjustable sample table located below the fiber. The fiber was attached to a robotic arm (Rotrics DexArm, Rotrics, USA). The LM-10 thermopile sensor from Coherent USA measured power at the fiber end before each ablation test to confirm that test conditions remained constant.
